What is our experience in the North-west ? Each and every one of the branch lines which we have constructed there has been absorbed by the main line, and it has been the experience of many countries that the construction of a number of railways does not of itself tend to reduce the rates. New railways will facilitate settlement and open the country, but when it comes to freight rates, these rival lines bind themselves together, and it is impossible to obtain the reduction in rates desired, except where the government intervenes with the object of benefiting the people and fixes a rate which will control the rates charged by existing lines through the same territory. In view of the large extent of line which the government is undertaking to build and the grave doubt as to the paying character of that line, it would have been far better for the government to have undertaken the building of this whole railway, and thus afford to the people of the North-west the undoubted benefits which low freight rates would confer upon them. Let me call the attention of the House to the fact that the theory is rapidly gaining in the American republic, that the time has arrived for governments to cease giving aid to railways, and in the constitution of a great majority of the states there is a provision against granting state aid to any railway. In Canada, where great reasons do not exist as in the present case, for the government intervening, we should refrain entirely from aiding railways in any shape or form.
The hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) has laid great stress upon the advantages of an all rail route for carrying grain. My information is that the vast bulk of the grain of the North-west is carried out of that country during the season of navigation, and it is an axiom in trans. Mr. MONK.
portation that grain can be carried by water at a far cheaper rate than it can be carried on railways. It is a known fact that to-day grain is carried from the western part of Lake Superior to Depot Harbour, to Midland, in fact to the eastern side of the great lakes, a distance of over 600 miles, for li cents, or, as I am informed, 1 cent a bushel; whereas the cost of carrying grain from Winnipeg to the shores of Lake Superior, a distance of 400 miles, amounts to over 12 cents per hundred weight, although I believe it is to be reduced to 10 cents on the 1st of October next, under the arrangements made by the Roblin government, or six times the cost per bushel of what it is over the waterway. The bulk of the grain being carried out during the season of navigation, and the rates being as they are, it seems to me that it is impossible for any railway, even constructed under the most favourable circumstances, to rival the navigation route; and as a result of that state of things, we find that scarcely 6 per cent of the grain which comes from the North-west is carried by rail. As a matter of fact, almost the whole of that grain avails itself of the water route; and therefore it is evident to me that the government, in the hasty course they have pursued in connection with this scheme, have failed to consider sufficiently the immense importance of the natural route which we have for the conveyance of that grain the moment it reaches the shores of Lake Superior down to the ocean ports within our own territory, whence it may be shipped abroad. I am informed that last year the amount of grain received by water in the city of Buffalo from the city of Chicago, a distance which could easily have been covered by rail, exceeded 74,000,000 bushels; which is proof once more, if any proof were required, that the navigation method of carrying grain will for a very long period in the future be superior to the rail-carrying method. Under these circumstances, after having spent such large sums as we have spent in improving our water routes from the lakes down the St. Lawrence to the city of Montreal, after having spent millions in the construction of canals, with the great question still unsolved-but I hope not entirely abandoned, of a canal along the Ottawa river, that canal known as the Georgian Bay canal-it seems to me that the government have been very hasty in arriving at the conclusion involved in the scheme proposed by the right hon. leader of the House. When we reflect on the large amount we have spent on the Intercolonial Railway, when we recollect what the attitude of this government was in 1897, when that road was extended from Levis to Montreal, the reasons advanced at that time by this government, and the hope entertained by the country generally that that step was only the first towards

carrying out the larger scheme of extending the Intercolonial Railway to the shores of the great lakes, it seems to me that in this project we are launching upon far too great an expenditure, an expenditure which the data at our command and under our observation does not in any sense justify.
Let us for a moment consider what is the cost to which we shall be put by the carrying of the railway through the mountain section. In this connection it is worthy of note-it has been stated already in this House-that there has been no demand in the province of British Columbia for the construction of this transcontinental railway. In regard to that province we have fulfilled every pledge to which we were bound when it entered confederation. We have never heard in this House any demand from that province for anything further in the way of a transcontinental railway ; but we have heard many demands for railways within the province, and any one who knows anything about the condition of affairs there knows that in order to utilize the large mineral wealth which that province possesses, it is necessary to build within the limits of the province railways to which possibly aid may be expected from this government. But taking the project itself, I think we may fairly assume that in connection with the mountain section we shall be obliged to furnish the full extent of the guarantee which is contemplated by the contract, and that section will cover a distance of about 600 miles. Those who have taken the trouble to refer to the very able report made by Sir Sanford Fleming in 1877, will find in that report a reference at length to the pass which it is contemplated that this Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will cross when entering the province of British Columbia through the Rocky mountains. He will find that Sir Sanford Fleming estimated the cost of the construction of that line at over $50,000 a mile ; and we may safely assume that under the present conditions of labour and the increased cost of materials, that estimate can be in no way reduced. We have, therefore, to furnish a guarantee of $30,000 a mile for a distance of 600 miles, amounting in the aggregate to $18,000,000. The interest upon that sum at 3 per cent for ten years, which is the time limit during which we may be expected to pay the interest, amounts to $540,000 a year, or, for the whole ten years, $5,400,000. That is the extent of our liabilities in regard to the mountain section, and I think the House will easily come to the conclusion by the time this discussion has advanced a little, that the estimate of $13,000,000 as being the total amount of cash payments which this government will have to make in connection with this contract, is far below the true mark. Five million four hundred thousand therefore is the amount which we will have to pay in connection with the regular mountain section, a section of railway for which no cry has been heard from the distant province of British Columbia.
Leaving the section of railway which traverses the prairie and) the Rocky mountains and coming to that portion which the government is to build, what do we find ? My right hon. friend has given us a most attractive picture of the region which that railway is to traverse on its way from Winnipeg to Quebec. Where did he get his information ? Where does he find his proof that this region is rich in agricultural lands, mineral resources, water powers and forests ? I have examined the report of Sir Sanford Fleming, and I do not find in that report anything to corroborate the glowing description given by my right hon. friend. The surveyors and engineers found here and there settlers who had grown vegetables. They found in places some rich agricultural soil, and they found trees in abundance, but we have no evidence whatever that the land is so adapted for settlement and that the climatic conditions are such as will justify our spending over $50,000,000 in the construction of a railway across that country. Nothing in that region, as far as I have been able to find, justifies in any sense the description given by my right hon. friend. And if we turn to later reports, there is one to which I may invite attention. I refer to the report of the survey and exploration of Northern Ontario in the year 1900. Although there is a rather flattering general summing up of the reports of the surveyors, who were deputed by the Ontario government to visit that region north of Lake Superior, it is impossible to go through these reports one by one and come to any other conclusion than that the greatest doubt exists as to the utility of that region as a place of settlement, which will justify the expenditure contemplated. I have no desire to belittle that region any more than I would the corresponding region in my own province, but we have not yet sufficient information to justify us in saying that it is one which should claim our attention at present'in lieu of other regions which we know something about. The same remark will apply to that portion of my own province intended to be traversed by this railway. A very interesting movement has been in progress in the province of Quebec since several years. The exodus of the people of that province to the United States has not diminished in a noticeable degree, but within the past few years a group of patriotic men in the province of Quebec, irrespective of party, men who have no private interest to serve, who have only one object in view, the keeping of our own population within our province, have been at work obtaining the moral assistance and help of the citizens of the province of Quebec. And what have these men achieved ? They have found back of the city of Montreal, in the great region

watered by the Saguenay river and Lake St. John and the rivers flowing into that lake, millions of acres which are unoccupied at present. But that region, to which we should at present devote all our attention, is not the region to be traversed by this railway. The region which this railway will cross is one unknown to us and unknown also to the right hon. gentleman. It is impossible for him or any member of the government to give us any precise information regarding the country where this railway is to pass, far beyond the height of land in the province of Quebec, over 200 miles from Montreal and 80 miles from the most distant settlements, such as St. Gerard de Montarville and St. Michel des Saints. This road will run fifty miles away from that region, and therefore will be of no help whatever to these men who are ready to lay before the government clear and precise information regarding this vast and unsettled region in the province of Quebec, to which they are seeking to attract our compatriots and prevent them from going to the States. That is the position with regard to the province of Quebec. There is not a man in the province of Quebec who has taken any interest in that great and noble movement inaugurated there some years ago for the purpose of settling the northern portion of that province and that portion from the shores of Lake Temiscamlngue down to the centre of the peniusula of Gaspe, who would not stand dumfounded if you proposed to him, as a help towards the carrying out of that patriotic scheme, a line of railway passing over one hundred miles from any known region in that province. And upon that score, if upon no other, I, for my part, do condemn that part of the railway which it is alleged is intended to help us towards these settlements of the province of Quebec, but which can be of no help whatever. Mr. Speaker, that movement to which I have referred, which perhaps exists in some degree in the province of Ontario, but I think not in the same degree as it exists in our province, for the same conditions do not present themselves -that scheme of settlement of our province covers the whole valley of the Ottawa, it extends throughout the entire valley of the St. Lawrence, north and south, and, as I stated a moment ago, it extends down to the county of my hon. friend from Gaspe, where, as I was informed when I visited that region, a few miles from the coast in the interior of that great peninsula, there is a fertile plateau in which there is room for over fifty parishes of settlers. This being so, what aTe the present needs of the province of Quebec if we wish to stem that tide of emigration to the United States which has been flowing so long? What we need in our province is colonization roads to afford easy access to those regions which are known to us, and the only obstacle to the settlement of which is the want of Mr. MONK.
proper means of communication. And I venture to say here that we do not need great expenditure. In other words we are expending $15,000,000 perfectly uselessly on the construction of a line and the effect of that construction, view it as you may, cannot but be a cause of injury to the Intercolonial Railway.

My hon. friend is under a misapprehension as to the charter obtained for a railway In the county of Gaspe. The line for which a Charter was obtained will run from Causapscal to Gaspfi Basin, but I think he refers to another charter which was obtained from the Quebec legislature during last session for a line running from Fraserville to Paspebiac. If he refers to that charter I can tell him that I am not interested in it.

I did not say my hon. friend was interested in it, but I am strongly of the impression that there are special charters given for a line running from Riviere du Loup or Fraserville-these places are very close to one another-and covering this country, because this is an admirable country for settlement and it requires a railway. By building that cut-off of 110 miles the distance will be shortened by 60 miles even if we left in Moncton. But we are building 400 miles of railway at a cost of $15,000,000 just to save 23 miles. Our own road is a good road. The road from Levis to Matapedia and even to Moncton is a very much improved road as compared with former days and can carry very great loads of freight. I fail to see what can possibly justify us in rushing hurriedly into the construction of a line as to which we have no information. It is not located, we have no survey, we have no estimate, but we are safe in saying that line cannot cost less than $37,500 per mile. It crosses, I believe, three watersheds, a great number of hills, a range of mountains and it passes through a country where construction is very difficult; in fact, even with this expenditure, I question very much if it will be possible to give to that line the easy grades and solid road-bed that our own Intercolonial Railway has for 423 miles between Levis and Moncton with the cut-off at Rivi6re du Loup. Now, I have promised to be short and I wish to conform to the precepts so well laid down and so ill-observed by the hon. member for North Norfolk, but I wish to say that it seems to me under these circumstances to be an immense expenditure. It seems to me that with an expenditure of $65,000,000 on the eastern

section of the road from Winnipeg to Quebec, say what you like as to our receiving interest upon that amount, we are borrowing the amount, we are increasing the public debt, and, although we own the property-property as to the value of which I have grave doubts-still, we owe that amount and therefore I think it is right to continuously bring the attention of the House and of the country generally to this enormous expenditure.
I cannot refrain from expressing my regret that since the expenditure is to he incurred we have not reserved unto ourselves not only the ownership but the management of the whole line from the Atlantic to the Pacific. The ideas which my hon friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) expressed so often when I was first in this House, have gained ground to an extraordinary degree. They are occupying the public mind throughout the world and I have no doubt that before many years we will regret this transaction by which we have alienated from our control this transcontinental line for at least fifty years. I therefore view with regret that part of the contract. And, Sir, corporations have no souls. This road is passing under the control of a company whose capital is not in this country; it' is English capital and that capital as employed in this country is entirely under the control of American management. X make no imputation whatever against the men who are leading in the management of the Grand Trunk Railway, but there is no doubt that the Grand Trunk Railway will control this corporation and certain it is that ultimately the control of this line will be in the hands of the Grand Trunk Railway and that management is American. They have vast interests in lines in the United States. They own lines in the United States and they have spent millions in improving their terminals at Portland and it would be very difficult for people who know something of that company to believe that they are ready to abandon these terminals. I believe myself that with the facility of outlet that they have they will find means of escape from the elastic clause in the contract in regard to Canadian commerce, Canadian ports, and a Canadian highway, and under these circumstances and knowing with the limited experience at my command how difficult it is to control the operations of these great railway corporations I say it is a matter of regret for me that the control has been given to the Grand Trunk Railway Company and I believe that before long a very strong conviction will exist throughout this country, at any rate in my own province, that we would have done better if we had determined to take up our Intercolonial Railway where it is and to bring it at a cost of less than fifteen million dollars to the shores of Lake Superior, to improve our waterways, to improve our ports, to im-268
prove the St. Lawrence route, and spend the rest of the money which I claim we are going to waste in an unknown country, there instead of spending it in a region as to which we have insufficient data.

Mr. Speaker. There is one ground upon which this great project may be opposed with some appearance of reason, and I congratulate my hon. friend (Mr! Monk) on having discovered it. We are submitting to parliament a proposal for the construction of a great transcontinental railway stretching from ocean to ocean through British territory, and about 3,500 miles in length. A portion of that line will run' through the prairie lands of Manitoba and the North-west; a country which nobody questions is in need of railways. These Prairie lands are fertile and fruitful, and we all recognize that they will supply traffic to a railway. But after all, that is only a small part of the scheme. This line starting from the very heart of the settled districts of the lower provinces, after leaving the city of Moncton will plunge into the unsettled interior of New Brunswick; thence, turning the corner of American territory, it passes through the settled lands of the province of Quebec, reaches the St. Lawrence at Levis, and crossing the new bridge will pass through the historic ancient capital of Canada, and thence once more plunge into new and undeveloped territory. Again in the far west, it will touch Winnipeg, and once more plunge into new territory, and so on and on, always touching far as practicable at the large centres on the way, but always striking out again into new and yet undeveloped Canadian lands.
Now, Sir, if we were to believe that this vast area of Canadian territory is a miserable, worthless and God forsaken country ; if we were to believe that such are the . conditions prevailing in 3,500 miles across this Canada of ours, then hon. gentlemen opposite are right in opposing this measure. But, if on the other hand, we believe that this line will open up new districts valuable for agriculture, if we believe that it will open up valuable tracts of timber-more valuable to-day than ever before when we consider the fast diminishing forest areas of this continent-if we believe that it will open up rich mineral districts - in Ontario, and Quebec, and through tbe mountains of British Columbia which are known to teem with mineral wealth; if we believe that it will bring into industrial use the vast water-powers of this Dominion which become more and more valuable every day as science advances; if we believe that throughout this 3,500 miles of country we have a territory worth owning, then we must believe that this is a good scheme, and, Sir, we are proud to proclaim ourselves as supporters of it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext: Hear, hear.

We are told by hon. gentlemen opposite that we are approaching this project without information, and we are asked if there are any surveys. Let me ask these gentlemen : Dffi they require surveys when in the year 1871 the Conservative party accepted the responsibility of building the Canadian Pacific Railway, and of making it a part of the treaty with British Columbia 1 We have more information concerning this proposal to-day than Canada had in 1871 when she accepted the responsibility of that treaty. If there be any difficulty to be met with in this case, it is not because of lack of information, for there is abundance of information. The greatest difficulty which gentlemen opposite will experience will be in digesting the great mass of matter bearing on this question which can be found in the archives of the public library.
The eastern part of the line was surveyed many years ago; the country between Winnipeg and Quebec has been examined and reported upon to a very large extent by competent explorers. The prairies are no longer an unknown land. The mountain passes of British Columbia have been examined and their character is well known and understood. Though we may have no locateu line to assist us, yet as the Prime Minister said, there are mountains of information available to those who will take the trouble to seek it. To state that we have no information on this subject is absolutely unjustified by the facts.
I suppose, Sir, that if there is one part of this scheme which is being more strongly opposed than another, it is that part of the railway which it is proposed shall run from Moncton to Quebec. I have no doubt that in the western part of the Dominion we shall hear that talked of more frequently than any other section, but at the same time I have no doubt that down in the eastern provinces we shall hear a great deal about this worthless country in Ontario which we are going to build a railway through. And, notwithstanding the speech of my honourable friend the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals, I do not think we shall hear much in the maritime provinces against this project of a railway from Moncton to Quebec. However, I fully expect that when the time comes when we have to meet our opponents on the platform in the lower provinces, we shall hear a great deal about the wild country in Ontario in which we are to squander money. Be that as it may, we have to ask our friends in the east and in the west to give and take in this matter, and to believe that in both cases the country is not so worthless as it is represented to be, but that it is a country worth owning and worth developing. One would think from what has been said about this Moneton-Queliee section that it was absolutely new and unheard of, a mad and a crazy scheme. We are asked, who

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
shall be so mad as to ask that another railway should be built from the waters of the St. Lawrence down to the lower provinces ? Well, Sir, so far as this part of the scheme is concerned, the line upon which it is proposed to build this road today, is practically one of the three main lines that were examined, and reported upon, and recommended by the surveyors for the Intercolonial Railway as far back as 1864. And yet, gentlemen opposite seem to treat this project to-day as something new and unheard of. We have some information about it in the report of Sir Sanford Fleming, made nearly forty years ago. We are told to-day that this road will be of no value. At that time Sir Sanford Fleming pointed out that the shortest line and the most direct line for through-freight that can be obtained from the Gulf of St. Lawrence to the lower provinces, is by what was called the frontier line running close to the state of Maine, and then he said, that next to that there was the ' central line,' and the ' central line ' of Sir Sanford Fleming's report is substantially and practically the line on which it is now proposed to build the railway. These are Sir Sanford Fleming's words :
The central route would, next to the frontier line, be the best for the transportation of through-freight, and as a means of colonizing the country and developing its natural resources it would stand in the first position.
Hear, hear.
That does not mean that the soil is not inferior by comparison.
By comparison with what ?
The hon. gentleman has just read that it is not by reason of it being so much more uncultivable, but by being inaccessible, which, of course, means that it is not as cultivable as other land.

Well, Mr. Speaker, all the lands of Canada are not equally fertile or valuable to the farmer ; but even if they are not all equal to the lands of the prairies, there are millions of acres in Canada which we expect to be occupied by settlers, millions which are to-day occupied .by settlers, even though they may not be what the hon. gentleman would call the superior lands. I will quote further from Sir Sanford Fleming's report of 1S64. I may say that there are three routes described-the frontier route near the state of Maine, the central route, which is the subject of the present discussion, and the route along the Baie des Chaleurs, which was afterwards adopted for the Intercolonial Railway. Sir Sanford Fleming says :
The central route will have the least population to accommodate Immediately along the line. Indeed, between the Mirarmichi and St. Lawrence there is only one settlement, which consists of a few families on the Tobique river. By opening roads, however, to the east and west, the county of Restigouche and the valley of the St. John *would be easily reached and a considerable portion of the trade of these sections brought within the influence of the railway. A line through the centre of New Brunswick would take the supplies for the lumber trade and would rapidly settle up the large tracts of cultivable land in this district.
You see, he considered it quite cultivable.
A railway so situated would, as a line of communication, have similar effects on the trade and progress of New Brunswick as the River St. John has had, with this additional advantage, it would be open all the year instead of half of it.	'
In much less time, it is believed, than has been occupied in settling and improving the lands which nature made accessible by the river, would the artificial means of communication result in populating the interior of the country through the greater part of its length, and thus develop and foster a traffic which does not now exist.
Such was the view held by Sir Sanford Fleming as far back as the year to which I have referred.
The cry lias been raised that this line should be objected to because it parallels the Intercolonial Railway. We claim that it does not parallel the Intercolonial Railway ; but for the sake of argument, we will assume that it does. Is that a conclusive argument against its construction ? I>o we refuse to parallel lines in this country ? Have we not granted parallel charters and parallel subsidies all over Canada? Have we not, during this very session, laid down the policy in the Railway Committee 268*
that charters may be granted for parallel railways so long as they are thirty miles from other railways ? Where has this parliament laid down the principle that we shall not grant charters or subsidies or assistance of any kind to parallel lines ? If we are prepared to grant parallel charters and subsidies in other cases, why not in the case of tlip Intercolonial Railway V What reason is there for treating the Intercolonial Railway in a different way from other railways in that respect ? Am I to be told that it is a good thing to parallel company roads, but a bad thing to parallel the Intercolonial Railway ? Am 1 to be told that because this is a government road we must nurse and protect it, and give it freedom from competition which private capital has to submit to ? Are we to tell investors in the railways of this country that they shall have their capital imperilled by charters and subsidies to other railways, but that we shall take care that our own road shall not be subjected to any such competition ? Surely we are not prepared to take that ground. Surely, if we grant charters and subsidies for parallel lines in which private capital is invested, there is no reason why the Intercolonial Railway, because it happens to be a government road, should be free from the competition which other roads have to submit to.
Suppose that instead of having built the Intercolonial Railway around the north shore, this favourable report of Sir Sanford Fleming had been adopted, and the Intercolonial Railway bad been built by this central route, what would have been the position to-day ? Undoubtedly the towns on the north shore would always be of some consequence, on account of their accessibility to the ocean ; but without railway communication they would not be in the flourishing condition that they are in today. Some of the prosperity that has come to them by reason of the railway communication they enjoy would have come to the people who would have settled along the central route, and that country would have been opened up and developed in the manner suggested in Sir Sanford Fleming's report. What then ? If the people of the north shore were coming to this House today and asking for a government grant of subsidy, or for government construction, or for some other means of giving them the benefit of railway communication, would we be able to meet them with the statement :	' Oh, no, we cannot give you a
railway, because it will parallel the Intercolonial ' ? Surely we would have been bound to extend to that section of country in the course of time the benefits of railway construction. And as in the beginning we built the Intercolonial Railway by the north shore and gave the people there the benefit of railway construction, surely the time lias come, whether it will parallel the Intercolonial Railway or not-and I want to

deal with the worst view of the case- when we would be justified in building a railway through that unsettled country which has been described so well in the report of Sir Sanford Fleming.
Well, Sir, does the proposed railway parallel the Intercolonial Railway 1 That question has been dealt with by my right lion, friend the premier, and there Is no need of my dwelling upon it. From the way in which this expression, paralleling the Intercolonial Railway, has been used, one would think that because two roads start from a common point and end at a common point, they may be said to parallel each other, even though they go around the opposite sides of a circle. There is no paralleling of the Intercolonial Railway by this road. After it leaves L6vis it is out of the way of the Intercolonial Railway at once. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) says that it never gets farther away from the Intercolonial Railway than fifty miles. I am advised by competent authorities that there are places where it will be S8 miles from the Intercolonial Railway.
Will it not take a large share of the trade which now goes over the Intercolonial Railway to Quebec ?

I am prepared to say that even if it does, that is no argument against the construction of the railway. When the Canada Atlantic Railway was the only line running directly from Montreal to Ottawa, and we were asked to aid the Canadian Pacific Railway to construct a line between these two cities, we did not consider whether the two roads paralleled each other or not ; and after the Canadian Pacific Railway line was built, the company proceeded to parallel their own line with another one. To-day you have four railways between Ottawa and Montreal, if I may include the road running to Prescott, all aided hy the government of Canada, and nobody seems to be very much aggrieved over the question of any of them being paralleled. Whether the Intercolonial Railway is paralleled or not, and whether this new road will take traffic from it or not, affords no argument against building the new line, opening up a new section of country, and doing something towards settling the unoccupied lands of the province of New Brunswick. If a road starts from Montreal or Quebec and runs to a point in the maritime provinces, and another railway which it is proposed to construct between those points is to be regarded as a case of paralleling, what happened when the Intercolonial Railway was paralleled in that sense by the construction of the short line of the Canadian Pacific Railway ? Did toe hon. gentleman stop to see whether it took any traffic away from the Intercolonial Railway ? No, that question did not count for anything then. There was no question then about paralleling

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
the Intercolonial Railway, or about competition with the Intercolonial Railway. Nobody cared anything then about the rights of the Intercolonial Railway, and our hon. friends in opposition were prepared to spend money liberally in building another line, which was not even a line completely on British territory.
There was another phase to that scheme. When it was adopted by the Conservative government, it included a branch which was to run from Harvey to Salisbury. Salisbury is a station close to Moncton, so that the Harvey and Salisbury line was of the same character as the one we are proposing to build now. The only [DOT]difference is that ours is to start in Quebec and go direct to Moncton, and the other was to start at a point further down on the line of the Canadian Pacific Railway and cross from Harvey to Salisbury. Why ? To serve the very purpose for which our projected road is intended to-day, namely, give another short line to the maritime provinces. There was no talk then about paralleling the Intercolonial Railway.
Was that a trunk line ?

I do not see that that makes any difference. It was a line which was going to carry freight, and might have taken freight from the Intercolonial Railway, but that never worried the souls of the hon. gentlemen who sat behind the government of that day. There is another view of the case. This so-called Har-vey-Salisbury line was deemed to be of so much importance to the maritime provinces that I believe I am justified in saying that but for the putting of that section into the scheme the Bill would have never been carried through parliament. I am assured of that by people who were familiar witli the facts at the time, and I do not believe that you would have had a member from the eastern part of New Brunswick or from the province of Nova Scotia, on either side of politics, who would have voted for that scheme at that time had they not the assurance that that line was to be built. Well, as in many other cases, the expectations created by hon. gentlemen opposite were not realized. The Harvey-Salisbury line was not built by the Canadian Pacific Railway. Then the maritime province members began to complain to the government of that day that faith had not been kept with them, that they had been misled, humbugged and deceived ; and in the efforts to conciliate, the government of,that day brought forward a Bill to construct the Harvey-Salisbury line ns a government work. That line was to reach the very point we are now reaching, because Salisbury is a station but a short distance from Moncton. Although the starting point was not the same the object was the same, namely, to get a short line to Moncton. What followed ? The Bill passed this House, but by some misfortune

it failed to pass the Senate, and there the matter ended. The good people of the maritime provinces were humbugged. They were humbugged first by putting the building of this line into the Canadian Pacific Railway arrangement, and afterwards by putting it into a special Bill, which was quietly so managed that the Senate threw it out. Is it surprising that from that day to this there has been, in a large portion of the maritime provinces, deep discontent on this question of the short line ? The maritime provinces have not been content with the short line which runs through the state of Maine. We have no objection to that line. We have no quarrel with the Canadian Pacific Railway. But we say that it would have been a wise policy to have had a short line on British territory. That which the government of the party opposite intended to give but failed to give, a short line on British territory, this government, after the lapse of these years, has undertaken to provide as a part of a great national scheme and to make amends for the wrong done to the maritime provinces in the manner I have described.
If we were to judge from what was said yesterday by lion, gentlemen opposite and repeated to-day, this is a very mad Scheme, and one that was never thought of before. No engineer would ever contemplate such a line. No sensible person would ever dream of it. But I have already shown that it was recommended as a good line by Sir Sanford Fleming in the early days, and that the government of Sir John. Macdonald deemed a short line to Moncton so important that they incorporated it first in their arrangement with the Canadian Pacific Railway, and afterwards made it the object of a special Bill. But that is not the whole history of this matter. Later on there were other negotiations respecting this road. After the government arrangement fell through, the Grand Trunk Railway came forward, in association with the people connected with the Temiscouata road. They asked for a subsidy for the building of a line from Edmundston, which is on the Temiscouata road, down to this very place, the city of Moncton. Yet we are told that the scheme was a mad one. One would imagine, to hear lion, gentlemen opposite, that no sane man would ever dream of such a thing. Well, the Grand Trunk Railway, under the management of Sir Joseph Hickson, believed so much in that scheme that they entered into negotiation with the government. in association with the Temiscouata Railway Company, to construct it over the very route we propose to-day, only they proposed to begin at Edmundston instead of at Levis. They came here and sought a subsidy. I have information, on which I can rely, that Sir John Macdonald personally approved of that scheme and was willing to grant a subsidy of $10,000 per mile to the company to build that road. I
have reason to believe that my statement is well founded, and the men to whom the promise was made can be found, if it be disputed. I do not say the government as a whole made the promise, because in the final settlement influences were brought to bear which led to the scheme being abandoned. But why was it abandoned ? Was it because it would parallel the Intercolonial Railway ? Not a bit of it. It was abandoned, not because it would parallel the Intercolonial Railway, but because it would compete with the new Canadian Pacific Railway short line. That was why the government of that day refused to grant the desired aid. I am not making any accusation against the government of that day, nor am I finding fault with the Canadian Pacific Railway. That company had recently built a short line to the maritime provinces, and thought it a little too much that it should be met immediately by an opposing line. We can make some allowance for. the stand then taken by the Canadian Pacific Railway, but many things have passed since then, and I think the Canadian Pacific Railway have no reason to-day to view this scheme W'itli disfavour. Any anxiety which they had in the beginning of the enterprise no longer exists, and we have no reason to suppose that they are hostile to this scheme. We are told that it is a mad scheme, one which nobody has ever thought of. Well, the board of trade of the city of Quebec passed unanimously resolutions in favour of that scheme and calling upon the government to aid it. The board of trade of Halifax also passed resolutions calling on the government to support that scheme with the public money. The board of trade of Truro passed similar resolutions. Were all these people mad? I happen to have under my hand the resolutions of the board of trade of Truro, which I may quote as a sample of the public opinion which existed in the maritime provinces then in favour of the very enterprise which the government propose to-day. On the 14th of February, 1890, the board of Truro passed the following resolution :
On what day ?

On the 14th of February, 1890, St. Valentine's day. They passed this valentine and sent it to their representative at Ottawa :
Resolved, That the Truro Board of Trade learns with interest of the proposed extension of the Grand Trunk Railway system to the maritime provinces connecting with the Intercolonial Railway at or near Moncton, thus giving a competing line to the west as well as a short line and one on all British territory, and hereby requests the Dominion government to afford all possible aid to promote the success of the undertaking ; and further .
Resolved, That a copy of this resolution be forwarded to our Dominion representative at Ottawa for presentation to the government.
G. CLISH, President.
G. A. HALL, Secretary.

No wonder my hon. friend from Colchester (Mr. Gourley), whenever he stands up here, sounds a loyal note. He comes from a loyal town and tliis Is a loyal resolution. As I had the pleasure of knowing both gentlemen, I desire to say in fairness to them that they are both good, staunch Conservatives of the town of Truro.
No doubt, that will add materially to the scheme that was outlined by the Tories first.

It was outlined by the government of Sir John Macdonald, but like too many outlines these outlines faded away as time passed on. The lines were obliterated. They lasted long enough for the scheme to serve in one or two elections in the maritime provinces, but the promises made were never realized. What I wished to call your attention to, Mr. Speaker, is that in all these negotiations to which I have referred, the same thing is seen. In the negotiations with the Canadian Pacific Railway in the beginning they were to have a line which was to include a line from Harvey to Salisbury, which is near Moncton, and the Bill was carried through this House to build the line from Harvey to Salisbury, near Moncton. And the Grand Trunk scheme that I have referred to was to build from Edmundston to Moncton. In all these negotiations Moncton was the objective point, as it is to-day. Why is Moncton the objective point ? Some lion, gentlemen talk ns if the great object, and the only object was to build the shortest and most direct line to the ocean. And my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) asked yesterday if this government were going to build this Eastern line, why did they not build it by the shortest line to St. John. There was applause on the other side of the House. There are n number of reasons why Moncton is the right point. One of the reasons is that if you want to get the shortest line from the waters of the St. Lawrence to the Atlantic ocean, you will not go to St. John, because that is not the shortest line. My hon. friend from Charlotte (Mr. Ganoiig) will endorse this, because the shortest line from the waters of the St. Lawrence to the Atlantic is to the port of St. Andrews. Therefore, the idea that you must go to St. John, because it is the shortest line is an entire delusion. I know that some hon. gentlemen have been influenced by that. The shortest line to the ocean is an important consideration, but it is not the only question involved. Other interests are entitled to receive consideration, and they did receive consideration in making this arrangement. There are various reasons why we should go to Moncton. In the first place, it is the centre of the maritime provinces, as near as we can get it. The actual centre of population is further east, probably in the

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
county of my hon. friend from Cumberland, possibly further east in the county represented by my hon. friend from Colchester. But, to reach that centre you would have to parallel the Intercolonial; it would be an actual parallelling, and we do not propose to do that. Moncton is the most convenient centre of connection for the million of people in the maritime provinces. Now, important as the grain traffic is, and we all recognize its importance, it is only one object to be considered in the making of a national transcontinental railway. We may believe, we are bound to believe, that this million of people in the maritime provinces will have something to send back to the west, and besides, there is the passenger traffic which must be considered. We do not think it wise to single out one port and give it a monopoly. Moncton is the most convenient point, and from it all the ports in the maritime provinces are most easily accessible. It is convenient to St. John. It is nearer to St. John than it is to Halifax. So far as the ocean port is concerned, St. John Is placed on at least equal terms; as I say, it is nearer to Moncton than Halifax is. We must leave the two harbours to argue the question as to their respective merits: but Moncton is chosen because it is the central point of all the maritime provinces. There are other harbours besides Halifax and St. John that are entitled to consideration. Those who had the pleasure and advantage of hearing the discussion of the Grand Trunk Bill in the Railway Committee will remember that Mi-. Hays, the manager of the Grand Trunk Railway, when asked about the use of the harbours of the maritime provinces, said that if the western country developed at its present rate, as we have no doubt it will, the time is close at hand when we should need, not one, but three or four harbours to serve the traffic coming from the west. We are not building for to-day, we are building for the future as well as for to-day; and it was sound policy on the part of the government to take as their objective point a point on the Intercolonial Railway in the very heart' of the maritime provinces, which gives easy access to St. John on the one hand and Halifax on the other, as well as to Sydney and Louisburg, both of which are oit the line of railway communication, and to Country Harbour, w-hich is the objective point of a line of railway now under charter, and to Whitehaven, one of the harbours in the lower provinces which will take its place some day as one of our prominent Eastern harbours. The policy of the government is not to select one port, but to select a central point from which access may be had to all the harbours in the lower provinces. I think our friends in St. John have no reason to regret this; I am sure that St. John will profit largely by the construction of this line. As I have said, it is nearer to Moncton than Halifax is, and when the trains come down

from tlie west they are as likely, if they want to go to St. John, to go over this road as they would be to go over the Intercolonial, which is much longer. The people of St. John have shown great enterprise in the past. They have invested their own money in providing harbour facilities for the Canadian Pacific Railway, and I rejoice to know that they are reaping the reward of their enterprise. But they are dependent wholly upon the Canadian Pacific Railway. They have connection with the Intercolonial, but we know that the Intercolonial and its connection, the present Grand Trunk, have no connection with the great west, and therefore the Intercolonial is not in a position to deliver at St. John the traffic of the western country. With this road built, instead of being dependent on the Canadian Pacific Railway only, St. John will have two strings to its bow. Not a pound of traffic that goes to St. John now will be taken away, and St. John will stand its chance of getting a fair share of the new traffic to be created by this road. Halifax, with its peerless harbour, will have advantages which it has not hitherto enjoyed. Surely, Sir, the time has come, after years of deception, humbugging and trickery about the lines to the maritime provinces, that faith should be kept with these people, and they should have a through line running on Canadian territory from ocean to ocean.
' I have given you so much with regard to the history of the past. Perhaps, before six o'clock I may have time to say a word with regard to what is going on at present. We are told that this is a mad scheme, a wild scheme, that nobody would place faith in it, that no business man would believe in it. Bet me read a resolution passed on the 23rd day of July last, relating to this scheme :-

Mr. Speaker, when the House suspended its sitting at six o'clock I was making' some reference to what is called the Moncton section of this proposed road-the road from Moncton to the city of Quebec, I endeavoured to point out that this road would serve a good purpose in opening up a country, the development of which is desirable and necessary. I endeavoured to point out that there were no particular difficulties in the way of construction and that while opening up a country which is capable of development we would at the same time obtain a shorter line through the province of New Brunswick which certainly is not a disadvantage, but in regard to which we may all agree in saying, I think, Sa much the better. I pointed out that Moncton had been chosen as the objective point because of its central position, because it affords by means of the Intercolonial Railway easy access to all of the important harbours of the maritime provinces. Moncton is in the eastern portion of the province of New Brunswick within a short distance, comparatively speaking, of the Nova Scotia boundary. It is very close to the point of communication with Prince Edward Island. There are two principal channels of communication between the mainland and Prince Edward Island. One is from Pictou in the province of Nova Scotia to Charlottetown and the other is from Point de Chene in the province of New Brunswick across to Suinmerside. The crossing from Point de Chene to Summerside is at a point quite near to Moncton. The traveller going down there and desiring to cross to Prince Edward Island would leave the Intercolonial Railway at a point a very short distance from Moncton. So, in locating Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
Moncton as the central point we have a point in the eastern portion of New Brunswick, near the Nova Scotia boundary, in close touch with the communication with Prince Edward Island. In that way in so far as any one point can serve the purpose, Moncton seems to fill the bill better than any other place we could have named. I do not say in this connection that 1 agree with all that has been said with regard to the original location of the Intercolonial Railway. It is sometimes spoken of as a political location. I suppose that term may be used in a good sense or in a sense of reproach. I am inclined to think though that there were high political reasons which could be and were urged in favour of that location. For myself I do not hesitate to say that if to-day we could have only one line of communication between the upper and lower provinces, I should prefer to have the lino of the Intercolonial Railway around the north shore. If you could have only one line then that line should be chosen not purely for commercial reasons but for larger national reasons, and I may say even for imperial reasons. The selection of the north shore route for the Intercolonial Railway at the time of confederation was to some extent based upon national reasons and to some extent based upon imperial reasons. It was deemed desirable that the line should afford a channel of communication between the east and the west and that it should be a sufficient distance away from the American boundary to make it what we sometimes call a military line. I think that is a reason which the whole country will sympathize with. Then, there was an imperial reason in connection with finance. Owing to Canada's splendid position to-day her credit is of such high standing that we need not look for a guarantor or endorser when we go into any transaction ; our position is so good that we need not seek for an imperial guarantee or attach much importance to it. But, while that is the condition to-day with the magnificent prosperity which our country has enjoyed for a number of years, that was not the condition at the time of the union, and the imperial guarantee was then deemed of sufficient importance to play an important part in the transaction. It was deemed desirable that the imperial government should give a guarantee to assist the Intercolonial Railway. While I do not go so far as to say that they would have refused to give the guarantee if another location had been adopted, it is probably not too much to say that when the government did determine to locate that road around the north shore they knew it was agreeable to the imperial authorities who for imperial reasons favoured it. However, I take the position that if we could have only one line to the maritime provinces that one line should be practically the location near the north shore

of New Brunswick, and I do not join in the opinion of those who think now that a mistake was made.
My right lion, friend the leader of the government (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) in his reference to this Moncton line, dwelt for some time on what he regarded as an important feature in connection with the bonding privilege. He said that this line would make us more independent of our American neighbours. That view has been scoffed at by some hon. gentlemen who point out that we are not really dependent on our American neighbours because we have access to our own seaports by our Intercolonial Railway, and that there is also another line by which we can get down to the sea. Though we may be independent in a limited degree of our American friends, 1 think we ought to make it plain to them that we are determined to be even more independent than we are. There was no part of the eloquent speech of my hon. friend that I admired more than his statement to the effect that the best possible way to live on friendly terms with our brothers to the south of us is to have them understand that we are determined to be absolutely independent of them. It is true that in some respects that we have been more independent of them as respects the bonding privilege than perhaps they were aware of. But we have been told that, because the bonding privilege is a mutual one and because it is of advantage to American railways as well as to the railways of Canada, we need not be alarmed that any change will take place. I believe that the fact that a thing is of advantage to one set of people in the United States is not always conclusive evidence that that condition of affairs will continue. I have no doubt the high tariff of the United States is a burden to many people living in certain sections of the country, but; while the tariff operates with particular severity upon the people of this section, it is regarded with favour by the people of other sections and I have no doubt by the majority at large. So the people of any particular section are obliged to bear the burden for the common good, and I have no doubt that if it suited the policy of our American friends to carry out the threats they have repeatedly made of the abolition of the bonding privilege, the fact that such action would be injurious to one particular set of men or to certain railway companies would not prevent them from carrying out that policy. Therefore, I say it is desirable that we should give our American brethren to understand that Canada is resolved to work out her independence in these things, that the present proposal will promote this object, and that even if still another railway should be necessary we shall be prepared to construct it. The attitude that the government has taken upon this subject and the speech which my right hon. friend has
addressed to the House on the subject has already attracted much attention across the border, and there is a much keener appreciation of Canada's independence than ever before. I read to-day in one of the great journals of the United States, the ' New York Journal of Commerce,' not a political journal, but a commercial journal:
What more particularly interests and concerns us now is the determination of Canada, at whatever cost, to be independent of the United States for the means of reaching the eastern and western seas with the products of her territory	Our policy has been anything
but liberal, though a liberal policy would have been as much to our advantage as to that of Canada. If we exclude or restrict her trade, keeping it from passing freely into and over our territory, we must expect her to provide for it elsewhere and ought to admire the spirit and determination with which she does it.
That, Sir, is a specimen of what is being said in the journals of the United States to-day. I agree with the hon. gentlemen opposite when they say that we have not been wholly dependent upon the United States for the bonding privileges. I believe we had some levers, but I am strongly convinced that these levers would not be powerful in the event of a great movement arising in the United States which might take the form of hostility to our country. Therefore in the interest of Canada to-day, as well as in the future, it is well that we should let our friends across the border understand, that whatever measure of independence of them we have now we shall maintain, and that we shall increase that measure of independence by the line that we are now proposing, and should the necessity arise, we shall not shrink from providing another.

I have no idea, Sir, that I shall be able to settle the dispute as to the saving in mileage between Quebec and \Mtpnctou. I accept the compliment which my hon. friend of course

did not intend, because no doubt he forgot the fact that from the point of view of the artist and designer, the curve is the line of beauty..
Hear, hear.

Taking an air-line and allowing 35 miles for curvature, we would have 386 miles as against 496, which is the mileage from the Chau-diere to Moncton by way of the Intercolonial Railway. Having regard to the natural obstacles, what does the hon. gentleman say the saving is ?

I am advised that a line of about 400 miles will probably accomplish the distance. Taking an air-line and adding 10 per cent, as engineers do in an ordinary country, it would give 386 miles, but I am going to treat it for the purpose of my financial calculation as a mileage of 400, because I wish to be absolutely fair in any argument I shall make.
The section from Quebec to Winnipeg has also been the subject of much discussion, and efforts have been made to show that the country through which this road is to run, is a country unworthy of our consideration. I stated this afternoon that the only ground on which I think hon. gentlemen opposite could fairly oppose this road with some show of reason, would be upon the assumption that this vast territory is absolutely worthless. We differ from that opinion, and we think that the territory is deserving of 'development. We think also that the representations that have been made, as to the very expensive character of this section for railway building, are entirely mistaken. We believe that the information which is available justifies us in saying that that portion of the country, speaking generally of it, is not one of great difficulty for railway building, but is one through which a railway may be built at a very moderate expense, and that it has resources which we ought to develop in order that we may build up the Dominion at large.
In the course of the surveys that were made for the Canadian Pacific Railway, it was found that a railway north of Lake Nipigon could be built at a very moderate cost, but it served the purposes of the company to go along the shore of the lake, Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
where the construction was very expensive. I believe that the records will show that the Canadian Pacific Railway could have been built at a much less expense if it had been built on the elevated plateau which lies behind Lake Superior and Lake Huron. The information we have on that subject is very clear. There is no difficulty whatever so far as we can learn, in obtaining a good location there, and the only reason that location was not adopted by the Canadian Pacific Railway was, that they wanted to avoid building a long branch down to Lake Superior. The reports all go to show that while on the lake shore the country is rough, rugged, and unsuitable for railway construction, when you go back a short distance into the country the conditions are much more favourable. In Sir Sanford, Fleming's report of 1S74, he says :
Although the general aspect of the country-east of Lake Nipigon as seen from Lakes Superior and Huron, is precipitous and rugged, to the rear of this wild and rugged frontier the surface descends northerly in easy slopes. So much is this found to he the case that in passing from Lake Nipissing to Lake Nipigon through the entire country the ascent to the summit level will actually he less than that which is experienced in passing through Toronto across the peninsula of western Ontario, by either the Great Western, the Grand Trunk, the Grey and Bruce, or the Northern railways.
That region was surveyed by Mr. James II. Rowan, in connection with the government survey of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and this is what he says of the condition of that country :
The principal physical difficulties to be contended with in the construction of a railway throughout the whole section of country under consideration, are the great extent of water encountered on the route, its rocky character and inaccessibility It is nevertheless believed that a very direct line could be obtained with quantities of excavation and embankment not exceeding the average of railways already constructed in other parts of the Dominon. The last difficulty could be overcome to a considerable extent by means of the knowledge of the country already obtained. There are not many large rivers to he crossed on the line proposed, and of these not more than three or four will require bridges of 200 feet span. Timber of good quality and in sufficient quantity fcr the various purposes of a railway can be obtained either upon the line or in its neighbourhood. The gradients will be favourable too, in no case exceeding one foot per hundred, or 52'80 per mile. Of these maximum gradients the percentage will be small.
That is not so good a line as my hon. friend from North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) hopes we will get, but it is as good as a number of the lines we have in Canada to-day. Again Mr. Rowan says:
It is not a mountain range but merely an elevated plateau, and one remarkable peculiarity connected with it is in the numbers of lakes which occupy its summit, whose waters can easily be diverted and made to flow either the one side or the other.

Further on Mr. Rowan says :
The character of the country is very similar in the neighbourhood of either side of this elevated plateau, but outside that margin the difference as regards its adaptability for railway construction is very marked ; for while to the south it is broken up by hills of considerable altitude, with lakes intervening, of all shapes, sizes, and some of great depth, to the north it is comparatively level and swampy.
The greater portion of the country explored is covered with a dense growth of moderate sized timber, consisting of balsam, spruce, poplar, white birch, some tamarack, and occasional groves of white, but principally red pine, while at many points there are indications of valuable mineral deposits.
And in a foot note concerning mineral deposits, the report says :
Iron, copper, lead and gypsum in large quantities : silver also has been found ; and the Indians say there is coal or lignite, which statement is borne out to some extent by a remark of Mr. Bell's in a geological report on the Albany river.
Now, if I wish to dwell a little further on the condition of the country between Winnipeg and Quebec, I do so because I am satisfied that by and by, in certain sections of the Dominion, we shall bear not so much about the Moncton section, but we shall he told, as we were virtually told today by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) that that country is a subArctic country, that it is not fit for settlement, and that we should not attempt to build a railway through it.
'Mr. MONK. I do not think that my hon. friend is quite fair. I said that we knew nothing-about the country, and that there was nothing in the reports to confirm the statements of the Prime Minister.

My hon. friend is mistaken. We know a lot about the country. I have been giving him- information from the reports of the explorers and surveyors, who tell us what they know about it; and I am going to give him some more. The hon. gentleman says we know nothing about the country. Why, the whole country has been explored and surveyed for several years by parties sent out by the Ontario government, and here we have their published report. I shall not inflict a great deal of it on the House, but in order that those who have not access to it may know what they say about the country, I shall read some extracts from it :
The results of these extensive explorations, as detailed in the elaborate reports sent in by the surveyors, the land and timber estimators and the geologists, have fully justified the most sanguine expectations in regard to the natural wealth and fertility of northern Ontario and demonstrated the wisdom of the action taken, whereby some accurate knowledge of the character and extent of its enormous undeveloped resources has been acquired'. It has been established beyond controversy that in the eastern part of the territory north of the height of land
there is an immense area of excellent agriculture land, apparently equal in fertility to any in older Ontario, with an equable and temperato climate and an abundance of wood and water, which render the inducements it presents to those in search of homesteads as good as those offered anywhere else on the continent. The apprehension entertained by some that our forest resources were very limited has been contradicted by the exploration and estimation of extensive pine areas on the southern slope, as well as the location of great forests of spruce and other varieties of pulpwood north of the height of land, which will enable this province to take a leading position in the commercial -world as regards the growing and remunerative pulp and paper-making industry. While the geological examinations have not resulted in any new discoveries of economic minerals (and it was scarcely expected they would), they have been of -material service in identifying and establishing the character of the different rock formations and locating promising indications as a guide to closer investigations in the future. Analyses of the peat taken from the extensive deposits in Nipisslng have conclusively shown its high qualities and economic utility, and established the value of this great natural store of fuel, which will probably make it useful in the industrial development of the country.
Then, under the head of Agricultural Lands, the report says :
The great clay belt running from the Quebec boundary west through Nipissing and Algoma districts and into1 the district of Thunder bay comprises an area of at least 24,500 square miles, or 15,680,000 acres, nearly all of which is well adapted for cultivation. This almost unbroken stretch of good farming land is nearly three-quarters as great in extent as the whole settled portion of the province south of Lake Nipisslng and the French and Mattawa rivers. It is larger that the states of Massachusetts, Connecticut, Rhode Island, New Jersey and Delaware combined, and; one-half besides of the state of New York. The region is watered by the Moose river, flowing into James hay, and its tributaries, the Abbittibbi. Mattagami and Missinahie, and by the Albany and its tributaries, the Kenogami and Ogoke. Each of these rivers is over 300 miles in length, and they range in width from 300 or 400 yards to a mile. They are fed by numerous smaller streams, and these in turn drain numberless lakes of larger or smaller size, so that the whole country is one net-work of waterways, affording easy means of communications with long stretches fit for navigation'. The great area of water surface also assures the country against the protracted droughts so often experienced in other countries. The southern boundary of this great tract of fertile land is less than forty miles from Missinahie station on the Canadian Pacific Railway ; and the country north of the height of land being one immense level plateau sloping off towards James bay, the construction of railways and wagon roads through every part of it would he a comparatively easy matter.
Under the head of Climate the report
says :
Another important fact established by the explorations is that the climate in this northern district presents no obstacle to successful agricultural settlement. The information obtained completely dispels the erroneous impression that its winters are of Arctic severity

and its summers too short to enable crops to mature. The absence of summer frosts noted by the explorers and the growth of all the common vegetables at the Hudson bay posts must disabuse the public mind of this erroneous impression. The 50th parallel of latitude passes through the centre of the agricultural belt, and the climate is not much different from that of the province of Manitoba, lying along the same parallel, with this exception, of course, that the winter js tempered by the great spruce forests and the presence of so large a proportion of water surface. The country, too, has an abundance of wood for fuel, building and commercial purposes, and plenty of pure water every where.
